Dialogue: keep Russian dash-dialogue as printed; en uses double quotes, zh uses “ ”, ja uses 「 」. Ostap's ironic вы to Vorobyaninov is mirrored by 您 in zh and polite です/ます in ja, while students' ты is 你 and plain form; en marks the shift only through tone. [rank 11]

Names: one transliteration table for the whole book (en BGN-style without diacritics, zh 新华社 standard, ja katakana with long vowels); diminutives (Коля/Колька, Лиза) are the same name with a diminutive marker in the target, never a different name, and the narrator's epithets (концессионеры, компаньоны, предводитель) are fixed formulas. [rank 11]

Soviet acronyms and renamed places: expand by meaning plus Latin acronym at first occurrence (ZAGS, MUNI), keep the 1927 names of stations and streets as printed and give the modern name once in a short note; 'имени X' is always rendered as 'the X Hostel/Club' (en), '以X命名的' (zh), 'X記念' (ja). [rank 11]
Dialogue: en uses double quotation marks instead of Russian dashes; zh uses “”; ja uses 「」; the narrator's mock-solemn asides stay in the same register and sentence order. [rank 2]

Soviet portmanteau institutions (Старгуброзыск, Маслоцентр, женотдел, загс, ГПУ, АХРР): translate the meaning into a plausible institution name, add the Latin acronym in parentheses on first occurrence only, then reuse the translated name. [rank 2]

Names: en uses simplified BGN transliteration with patronymics kept (Ippolit Matveyevich); zh uses standard Xinhua transliteration with ·; ja uses katakana with ・; ты/вы is marked in ja by plain vs です・ます forms and in en/zh by tone, never by a note. [rank 2]
Dialogue: replace the Russian em-dash speech marks with the target convention (en double quotes, zh “ ”, ja 「 」); keep the narrator's interjecting dialogue tags in place. [rank 3]

Ostap's refrains (Лед тронулся..., Заседание продолжается!, конгениально, ключ от квартиры, Один мой знакомый...) are rendered verbatim identically at every occurrence in all three languages. [rank 3]

ты/вы: Ostap and Vorobyaninov use вы to each other (ja ですます, zh 您 sparingly); both use ты to the yard-keeper Tikhon (ja plain form, no honorific; zh 你); Japanese narration uses no honorifics on names. [rank 3]

Ostap's mock titles for Vorobyaninov (предводитель, председатель, директор предприятия, присяжный заседатель, душа общества) form a fixed set: each gets one rendering book-wide and is never smoothed into a neutral 'you'. [rank 15]

Dialogue: Russian em-dash lines become double quotes in English, “” in Chinese, 「」 in Japanese; Ostap's shift from вы to ты when abusing Vorobyaninov ('Пошел вон', 'Вот тебе') is marked in Japanese by dropping keigo and in English/Chinese by register, never by a note. [rank 15]
Forms of address: товарищ = comrade/同志/同志, гражданин = citizen/公民/市民, барышня = young lady/小姐/お嬢さん, applied consistently since the book jokes on the difference. [rank 15]

Soviet acronyms and trust names (Старсобес, губплан, Старгико, Мельстрой, Быстроупак, госпромцветмет): en transliterates and adds a two-word gloss in parentheses on first occurrence only; zh and ja give a compact institutional name with the transliteration in brackets on first occurrence, then the short form alone. [rank 5]

Dialogue: Russian keeps its em-dash lines; en uses double quotation marks, zh uses “”, ja uses 「」; narrator's mock-solemn asides stay in the same dry register with no added exclamation or softening. [rank 5]

Names: full name and patronymic are kept wherever the Russian has them (never replaced by surname or first name alone); ja uses ・ between parts and no honorific for narration, さん/どの only inside quoted speech; zh uses · and fixed syllabification per the glossary. [rank 5]

value.finding: Пенал is the ordinary Russian word for a schoolchild's pencil case: Ushakov defines it as an elongated wooden box for keeping pencils, pens and nibs. In chapter XVI ('Общежитие имени монаха Бертольда Шварца') the narrators use it as a running metaphor: the big mezzanine room is cut by plywood partitions into strips two arshins (about 1.4 m) wide, 'the rooms were like pencil cases, with the only difference that besides pencils and pens they held people and primus stoves', and thereafter the cubicles are simply 'пенал № 2', 'третий пенал', 'пятый пенал', 'крайний пенал слева', with the whole 'фанерное сооружение' shaking when a door is kicked. The joke is that the student housing of 1927 Moscow, with its acute shortage of rooms, reduces people to stationery in a box; it is mock-precise and deadpan, not slang, and the word had no special period meaning beyond the everyday object. John Richardson's standard English translation renders it consistently as 'pencil box' ('the fifth pencil box', 'box no. 2'). I could not verify online the wording of the Chinese (上海译文出版社 2022 and earlier editions) or Japanese (江川卓, 筑摩書房 1969) translations for this passage; the proposed 铅笔盒 and 筆箱 are the ordinary words for the object in each language.
value.rationale: All three keep the plain everyday object (denotation) and the deadpan metaphor (register), which the narrators themselves explain in the text, so no note is needed; 'pencil box' follows Richardson's established English rendering rather than the proposed 'pencil-case'. Bind the word once and use it for every recurrence ('the third pencil box', 'pencil box no. 2', 第三个铅笔盒, 三番目の筆箱); what is given up is only the arshin measure, converted to metres or feet in the surrounding sentence.

value.finding: Милиция was the ordinary uniformed police of Soviet Russia: the Provisional Government abolished the tsarist полиция and created a 'people's militia' by decree of 17 April 1917, and the Bolsheviks reaffirmed it on 10 November 1917 as the Workers' and Peasants' Militia (Рабоче-крестьянская милиция), reorganised as a regular state body in 1918. The name was ideological branding, chosen to distance the new force from the 'bourgeois' tsarist police, but by 1928 the institution was a salaried, professional, NKVD-subordinate police force, not a citizen volunteer body, and the word carried no 'militia' connotation for a Russian reader; it simply meant the cops, with the word полиция reserved for tsarist times (the narrators themselves contrast 'царская полиция' with 'советская милиция'). The name lasted until Medvedev's law renamed the force полиция on 1 March 2011. The 1961 John Richardson English translation renders it literally as 'militia' / 'militiaman'; Anne O. Fisher's 2011 translation has footnotes but I could not verify her choice online. Chinese coverage of the Soviet force gives 民兵 and 民警 as alternatives, with 民警 the customary reader-facing rendering (直译民兵, 国内一般翻译为民警); Japanese coverage uses 民警 with ミリツィヤ as a gloss and 警察 for the post-2011 police. (The prompt's mention of 2013, Durov and VKontakte appears to be a template error for this 1928 novel and was disregarded.)
value.note_for_reader: Soviet police were officially called militsiya ('militia') to mark a break with the tsarist police; the word meant ordinary uniformed police, not an armed citizen force.
value.rationale: English 'the police' keeps the denotation and the neutral everyday register that the word had for a 1928 reader and gives up the revolutionary naming, which a single note at first occurrence restores; where the text itself opposes tsarist полиция to Soviet милиция, render 'tsarist police' vs 'Soviet militia' once, with the note. Chinese and Japanese 民警 is the established rendering in both languages' coverage of the Soviet force and keeps both the 'people's' colouring and the police denotation, so nothing is lost there.

value.finding: Gambs is a maker's name: Heinrich Daniel Gambs (1765-1831), a German cabinetmaker trained under David Roentgen, came to St Petersburg in 1790, opened a workshop on Nevsky Prospekt in 1795, was named court mechanic in 1810 and supplied the Winter Palace, Pavlovsk and Tsarskoe Selo; his sons Peter and Ernst ran the firm until roughly the 1860s, after which it vanishes from directories. 'Гамбсовская мебель' became a byword in 19th-century Russian for expensive, fashionable, well-made furniture (Pushkin, Turgenev's Fathers and Sons, Goncharov's The Precipice all use it), so for a 1928 reader the phrase evoked a genteel pre-revolutionary drawing room and the old world Vorobyaninov has lost; the novel's own chairs are described as walnut with curved legs in English chintz, and the ironic touch is that the label 'Master Gambs, 1865' is a date by which the real firm had closed, i.e. a later imitation. English translations already treat it as a maker's name: Richardson (1961) writes 'Made by Hambs', Fisher (2011) 'a Gambs furniture set'. I could not verify a rendering in the published Chinese (Zhang Peiwen, 2004) or Japanese (Egawa Taku, 1961/1969) translations from what is online, so the zh and ja forms below are standard transliterations, not confirmed quotations.
value.note_for_reader: Gambs: St Petersburg court furniture firm (founded 1790s by Heinrich Gambs, closed by the 1860s); in 19th-century Russian 'Gambs furniture' meant luxury furniture, as 'Chippendale' does in English.
value.rationale: All three keep the denotation (a specific maker, used adjectivally like Chippendale or Thonet) and the neutral, matter-of-fact register; the connotation of faded pre-revolutionary luxury is not carried by the name in any target language and is supplied once by the note. 'Gambs' follows Fisher's spelling over Richardson's 'Hambs'; 甘布斯 and ガンブス are the standard transliterations, with 製 in Japanese to signal a maker rather than a style.

value.finding: A примус is a portable wickless pressure stove burning kerosene, invented in Stockholm in 1892 by Frans Wilhelm Lindqvist; the Swedish brand name became the generic Russian word for any such stove, and the USSR produced its own from 1922 (Kolchugino) with the design unchanged until 1990. Because of the early-Soviet housing shortage it was the standard hearth of the communal-apartment kitchen through the 1920s-30s, so for a Russian reader it evokes cramped kommunalka life: the roar and hiss of the burner, kerosene fumes, soot, and 'kitchen slavery' (it appears as the emblem of household drudgery in 1920s agit-posters, in Mandelstam's 1925 children's book 'Примус', in Zoshchenko, and above all in Bulgakov's Behemoth 'починяю примус'). In The Twelve Chairs it is exactly this: the pencil-box rooms of the Moscow communal flat 'with people and primuses', neighbours who light the primus so their kissing cannot be heard, Ostap telling Vorobyaninov to dry his dyed moustache 'in front of a primus'. Richardson's English translation (lib.ru) renders it 'primus stove'; in Japanese, プリムス on its own now reads as the Iwatani-Primus camping brand, and Japanese Wikipedia's headword is プリムス・ストーブ under the category 石油コンロ; in Chinese the transliteration 普里姆斯 is not established and translations of Bulgakov and Ilf-Petrov use 煤油炉.
value.note_for_reader: The primus, a roaring, hissing kerosene pressure stove, was the one cooking appliance of every 1920s Soviet communal kitchen; its noise and fumes are the sound and smell of shared housing.
value.rationale: English keeps the brand word because 'Primus stove' is the established rendering (Richardson) and is transparent to English readers; Chinese and Japanese give up the brand name (unknown in Chinese, and in Japanese it now means camping gear) to keep the denotation 'kerosene stove' in the plain everyday register the Russian has, letting a single note carry the communal-life connotation and the noise that the kissing joke depends on.

value.finding: «Красный мак» (The Red Poppy) is Reinhold Glière's three-act ballet, libretto by Mikhail Kurilko, premiered at the Bolshoi on 14 June 1927 as the first Soviet ballet on a modern revolutionary subject: a Soviet ship captain in a 1920s Chinese port, exploited coolies, and the dancer Tao-Hoa who dies giving him a red poppy. It was a runaway hit, over 100 Moscow performances by December 1928 and reportedly 200 in its first year, so in 1928 it was the fashionable new Bolshoi show every Muscovite knew (its Sailors' Dance became a standard). In chapter XVIII the narrator says sitting at the museum's giant desk would be like sitting at Theatre Square, where the Bolshoi 'with its colonnade and four bronze nags dragging Apollo to the premiere of The Red Poppy' would look like an inkstand: the joke pairs Klodt's classical quadriga with the topical agitprop ballet. The work was renamed «Красный цветок» (The Red Flower) in 1957 to avoid the opium association, which is why later Russian readers may know both titles. English coverage uniformly uses 'The Red Poppy'; Chinese Wikipedia and music sites use 《红罂粟》 (also 红罂粟花); Japanese Wikipedia heads the article 『赤いけしの花』 while publishers such as Zen-on use 《赤いけし》.
value.note_for_reader: The Red Poppy: Glière's 1927 ballet, the first on a Soviet revolutionary theme and the Bolshoi's hit of the season.
value.rationale: All three are the established titles of the ballet in each language, so denotation and the ballet-title reading are kept; the topical 'hit of the moment' connotation that made Apollo being hauled to it funny in 1928 cannot survive in the title alone, so a one-line note supplies it. For Japanese the fuller Wikipedia form 赤いけしの花 is preferred over 赤いけし as the more recognisable head title, though both circulate.

value.finding: Ostap Bender's signature exclamation, first spoken in Chapter VI ('Брильянтовый дым') of The Twelve Chairs (1928) when he and Vorobyaninov price the jewels, and repeated through the book and again in The Golden Calf. 'Лёд тронулся' (the river ice has started moving, i.e. the spring break-up) is an ordinary Russian idiom for 'things have finally started moving'; Bender welds it to 'господа присяжные заседатели', the formal address to jurors of the pre-revolutionary court (abolished in 1917), so a con man of 1927 is mock-solemnly addressing a defunct institution to an empty room, in the same vein as his 'Заседание продолжается!'. Both halves became proverbial and are quoted together, verbatim, to this day. Existing renderings: Richardson 1961 'Things are moving, gentlemen of the jury' (drops the ice); Fisher 2011 (Northwestern) 'The ice has started breaking up, gentlemen of the jury!' (per search snippet; not verified against the printed page); the commonest English gloss in commentary is 'The ice has broken, gentlemen of the jury'. Zhang Peiwen's Chinese (人民文学, 2004) uses '坚冰已破，诸位陪审员大人！' (with '众位陪审员先生' once, an inconsistency to avoid). No online text of Egawa Takashi's 1969 Japanese translation was found, so no established Japanese wording could be confirmed. The brief's reference to Durov/VKontakte 'around 2013' does not apply to this term; the searches found no link.

rendering.en: The ice has broken, gentlemen of the jury!
rendering.zh: 坚冰已破，诸位陪审员大人！
rendering.ja: 氷は動き出しましたぞ、陪審員諸君！

value.note_for_reader: Bender's catchphrase: 'the ice has started moving' (things are under way), addressed to the jury of the tsarist courts, which no longer existed in 1927.
value.rationale: All three keep the two-part shape (ice idiom + jury vocative) word-for-word so the line is identical at every recurrence and the mock-courtroom joke survives; en follows the commonest established gloss, zh binds Zhang Peiwen's proverbial 坚冰已破 form, ja keeps a literal 'ice has begun to move' since no established wording could be verified. Given up: the specifically Russian spring-break-up image and, in English, the slight interference from 'break the ice' (social sense); the tsarist-jury connotation is carried by the note rather than the wording.

value.finding: Elena Stanislavovna Bour, a prosecutor's widow born 1877, was Vorobyaninov's mistress in 1899 (he took her to Paris) and is now a card-and-coffee-grounds fortune-teller in Stargorod, living at Pereleshinsky Lane 7 with a white parrot in red underpants; her flat hosts the mock-conspiracy 'Union of the Sword and Ploughshare'. In the Russian text the narrator names her, then deflates her as 'гадалка' ('возопила гадалка'), 'хозяйка' and 'старуха' ('Она была старухой, была грязновата...', 'Старуха бросилась ему на шею'), the comedy lying in the gap between Kisa's 1899 memory and the present. John Richardson's standard English translation (1961, at lib.ru) keeps the name 'Elena Stanislavovna', titles ch. 10 'The Mechanic, the Parrot, and the Fortune-teller', and renders старуха as 'old woman' ('She was an old woman, she was dirty...') and хозяйка as 'hostess'. The 2022 Shanghai Translation edition (白桦熊) titles ch. 10 '钳工、鹦鹉和算命婆', so 算命婆 is the established Chinese word for гадалка; the character's Chinese name was not visible in any fetched page. No Japanese page showed the name or the fortune-teller wording of Egawa Taku's 江川卓 translation (筑摩書房 1969/1977), so the katakana is by convention, not attestation.

rendering.en: Elena Stanislavovna (гадалка: the fortune-teller; старуха: the old woman)
rendering.zh: 叶莲娜·斯坦尼斯拉沃夫娜（гадалка：算命婆；старуха：老太婆）
rendering.ja: エレーナ・スタニスラヴォヴナ（гадалка：占い師；старуха：老婆）

value.note_for_reader: Vorobyaninov's mistress of 1899, now a small-town fortune-teller; the narrator's flat 'fortune-teller' and 'old woman' are the joke, not an insult.
value.rationale: Keeps the name as a plain transliteration in all three languages and one fixed deadpan word each for гадалка and старуха (Richardson's 'fortune-teller'/'old woman', the Shanghai edition's 算命婆 plus colloquial 老太婆, Japanese 占い師/老婆), preserving denotation and the ironic register; the patronymic's pre-revolutionary politeness and the Polish flavour of 'Stanislavovna' are given up as untranslatable without a note.

value.finding: Title of chapter 12 of «Двенадцать стульев» and Ostap Bender's verdict on the widow Gritsatsueva, whom he marries for her chair: «Знойная женщина, — сказал Остап, — мечта поэта. Провинциальная непосредственность.» Serov's Энциклопедический словарь крылатых слов (2003) lists it as a крылатое выражение used шутливо-иронически of an emotional, fiery, temperamental woman; by 2013 it was a stock joke, reinforced by Natalya Krachkovskaya's Gritsatsueva in Gaidai's 1971 film. Established English: John Richardson (lib.ru text) titles the chapter 'A Passionate Woman Is a Poet's Dream'; Anne O. Fisher's Northwestern translation is cited as 'a passionate woman, a poet's dream'; English film coverage says 'a sultry woman and a poet's dream'. Chinese editions differ: Zhang Peiwen (人民文学出版社, 2004) titles it 「炽热的女人，诗人的幻想」, a WeRead edition 「热情似火的女人是诗人的梦想」. For Japanese (江川卓訳, 1966/1969) no chapter title or quoted line was found online; the ja rendering is unverified against print.

rendering.en: A Sultry Woman, a Poet's Dream
rendering.zh: 炽热的女人，诗人的梦想

value.note_for_reader: Ostap's mock-poetic verdict on the widow became a Russian catchphrase for a fiery, over-eager woman.
value.rationale: All three keep the two-beat epigram shape so the chapter title and the in-text line stay identical, and keep the mock-lyrical register that makes it quotable; 'sultry' is the dictionary sense of знойная and is attested in English coverage, though Richardson and Fisher chose 'passionate'. zh adopts Zhang Peiwen's 炽热的女人 but uses the plain 梦想 for мечта; ja keeps the heat image (灼熱) and gives up any claim to an established printed form.

value.finding: An уездный город was the seat of an уезд, the lowest administrative unit of the Russian Empire (from 1775), where the police chief and all district offices sat; the 1923–1929 Soviet reform abolished uyezds in favour of районы, so in 1928 the word was already dated, mildly old-regime. 'Город N' is a stock Russian literary toponym going back to Gogol (Dead Souls, The Government Inspector) and Chekhov: an anonymous, interchangeable backwater that stands for every provincial town; the Latin N is a convention, not a name, and readers recognise it instantly (in the war years the same device became 'Энск'). Ilf and Petrov open the novel with it deadpan, and the opening sentence is proverbial. Existing renderings: John Richardson's English (1961) 'the regional centre of N.', Anne O. Fisher's (Northwestern, 2011) 'the provincial town of N.'; the Chinese translation opens 'N县城的理发馆和寿材铺是如此之多…', so N县城 is established; the Japanese translation by 江川卓 (集英社 1966 / 筑摩 1969) could not be checked online, so no Japanese rendering is confirmed.
value.note_for_reader: 'Town of N': a Russian literary convention since Gogol for an anonymous provincial town; N is a placeholder, not a name.
value.rationale: All three keep the bare Latin N and the mock-solemn register; English follows Fisher's established 'provincial town', which carries the Gogol echo and backwater connotation but gives up the exact administrative rank (a 'district town' is smaller than a provincial capital); Chinese 县城 keeps rank and connotation at once; Japanese 郡の町 keeps the rank (уезд = 郡) and makes N the town, not the county, but gives up the familiar 'N市' pattern of Japanese Gogol and Chekhov translations.

value.finding: Novorostsement (Новоросцемент, a Soviet stump-compound of Новороссийск + цемент, not «New Russia») is a real organisation: the state cement trust formed on 5 February 1922 from the nationalised Novorossiysk cement works (plants Звезда, Цепь, Солнце, Пролетарий etc.), reorganised in 1925 as the North Caucasus State Association of cement and slate plants; it still exists as АО «Новоросцемент», the oldest working cement enterprise in Russia, and uses the Latin name «Novoroscement». In the novel it appears twice in Father Fyodor's letters (ch. XX: «Брунс служит теперь в Ростове, в „Новоросцементе“»; ch. XXVII: «„Новоросцемент“ — весьма большое учреждение, никто там инженера Брунса и не знал»), where the personnel office tells him Bruns was lured away to Azneft in Baku. For a 1928 reader the name was a typical piece of NEP-era institutional shorthand, a huge faceless трест whose 'личный стол' has a file but no memory of a man; the trust's head office was in Novorossiysk, and I could not confirm from sources whether it kept a board in Rostov (then the North Caucasus krai capital), so the Rostov location may be authorial licence. Existing English renderings: Richardson (1961) gives 'New-Ros-Cement', a half-expansion that wrongly suggests 'New Russia'; the 1930 Hill/Mudie abridgement (Diamonds to Sit On) omits the passage; the company's own English name is 'Novoroscement'. I found no accessible Chinese or Japanese published rendering.

rendering.zh: 新罗西斯克水泥托拉斯

value.note_for_reader: Novorostsement: the state cement trust of Novorossiysk (Black Sea port), founded 1922; a typical Soviet 'stump-compound' name, like Azneft.
value.rationale: English keeps the denotation and the acronym-jargon flavour by transliterating (consistent with the edition's ц→ts system; Richardson's 'New-Ros-Cement' mis-expands the place name); Japanese keeps the same flavour with the transparent loanword セメント so the reader hears 'cement' at once; Chinese, which does not transliterate Soviet stump-compounds, expands to the place name plus 水泥托拉斯, keeping denotation and the trust-era register but giving up the compressed acronym feel, and correcting 新罗斯 ('New Russia'), which the name does not mean.

value.finding: «Достойно есть» (Greek Ἄξιόν ἐστιν, Axion Estin) is the best-known Orthodox hymn to the Theotokos, named from its opening words «Достойно есть яко воистину блажити Тя, Богородицу…»; it is sung at the climax of the Divine Liturgy right after the consecration, and also closes many other services, so any Russian churchgoer of 1928 knew it by heart. In chapter 3 Father Fyodor locks himself in the bedroom and 'глухим голосом стал напевать «Достойно есть»' — a priest humming the most solemn Marian hymn of the Liturgy while scheming after a widow's jewels, which is the joke. John Richardson's 1961 English translation (lib.ru text) renders it as 'It Is Meet'; the standard liturgical English title is 'It Is Truly Meet'. The Japanese Orthodox Church's fixed title is 「常に福にして」 (ja.wikipedia, orthodoxjapan.jp). Chinese Orthodox usage has no one-word title: the current orthodox.cn Liturgy text opens the hymn «称你为有福，确实是理所当然的；永远蒙福、至洁无玷的诞神女…», and the 1910 prayer book gives «诚应为洵祝福尔生上帝者» under the heading 又圣母经. I could not access the Chinese (上海译文) or Japanese (江川卓, 1969) editions of the novel to check their wording, so the zh rendering below is built from the liturgical text rather than from an existing translation of the novel.
value.note_for_reader: «Достойно есть» / 'It Is Truly Meet': the hymn to the Mother of God sung at the most solemn moment of the Orthodox Liturgy; a priest humming it in private is a comic mismatch.
value.rationale: All three keep the denotation (a real, named liturgical hymn) and the formal church register; en and ja use the churches' own established titles, while zh, lacking a fixed Chinese title, pairs the generic 圣母颂 (so the reader knows what it is without a note) with the liturgical incipit 《称你为有福》 instead of the invented 《理当赞美》. What is given up is the instant recognition a Russian reader had, which the one-line note restores.

value.finding: In chapter XI ('Алфавит — зеркало жизни') the ордера are the paper vouchers of the Stargorod communal-economy office (Старкомхоз) by which furniture requisitioned from private houses in 1918-19 was handed out to institutions and individuals; the archivist Korobeinikov keeps the counterfoils (корешки), each bearing the recipient's address and signature, and for the Vorobyaninov suite there are five: one for ten chairs (to the Moscow furniture museum), two for one chair each, one for a round table, one for a tapestry. In 1920s Russian ордер was the standard bureaucratic word for a written authorisation to receive something (an ордер for a room from the жилотдел, an ордер for goods), so to a reader it connotes the requisition-and-allocation machinery of War Communism, not a command and not an arrest warrant. The 1961 Richardson English translation (lib.ru) renders it plainly as 'orders' ('the orders for the distribution of the furniture requisitioned from Vorobyaninov's house', 'the bundle of green counterfoils') and the term recurs as the treasure hunt's paper trail (stolen by Father Fyodor, shown to the museum curator). Search did not turn up the text of the Chinese (上海译文) or Japanese (江川卓, 1969) translations, so no established zh/ja rendering could be verified.
value.note_for_reader: An ордер here is a housing-office voucher recording who received a piece of requisitioned furniture, not a command or an arrest warrant.
value.rationale: Kept the denotation (an allocation voucher with a counterfoil) and the dry bureaucratic register in all three languages, and in English stayed close to the established 'orders' while adding 'distribution' to block the command/arrest readings; gave up the specifically Soviet flavour of the word, which 分配单 and 配給伝票 only partly recover (配給 carries a rationing overtone that suits the requisition era).

value.finding: Предводитель дворянства was the elected head of the noble corporation of a governorate or district (uyezd) in the Russian Empire, created by Catherine II's 1785 Charter to the Nobility, elected for three-year terms by the Assembly of Nobility, chairing that assembly and, later, zemstvo assemblies, conscription and school boards; the post was abolished in 1917. Vorobyaninov was a district (уездный) marshal, so in 1927 the title marks him as a лишенец-type relic: a provincial bigwig of a vanished order now a registry-office clerk. Ostap clips it to bare предводитель and uses it as a running vocative ('Молитесь, предводитель', 'Снимайте пиджак, предводитель', 'Как вы думаете, предводитель...'), and puns on the word's other sense, 'chieftain/ringleader', in 'уездный предводитель команчей' (ch. VI), at which Vorobyaninov takes offence and Ostap upgrades him to 'фельдмаршал'. Established equivalents of the full title: English 'marshal of the nobility' (Wikipedia; Richardson's 1961 translation, which renders the pun as 'District Chief of the Comanchi' and the apology as 'Field Marshal'); Japanese 貴族団長 (ja.wikipedia, standard in Russian-literature translation); Chinese 贵族长 (as in 县贵族长 in Anna Karenina character lists); the 2022 Chinese editions' blurbs use the looser 首席贵族. I could not verify from full text how Richardson or Fisher render the bare vocative, nor the exact wording in the 张佩文 (2004), 白桦熊 (2022) or 江川卓 (1966/69) editions. The prompt's mention of Durov/VKontakte coverage does not apply to this term and was disregarded.
value.note_for_reader: Marshal of the nobility (предводитель дворянства): elected head of a district's gentry before 1917; Ostap shortens it to 'Marshal' and uses it as a mock title, punning on its other sense, 'chieftain'.
value.rationale: All three keep the denotation via the established equivalent of the full title (marshal of the nobility / 贵族长 / 貴族団長), introduced in full once and then clipped to the fixed, faintly absurd honorific Ostap repeats; 'Marshal' also keeps the register (an obsolete rank that sounds military) and gains a Wild-West echo for the Comanche joke. Given up: the Russian word's plain 'chieftain/ringleader' sense that makes 'предводитель команчей' a pun rather than a mere juxtaposition, and in zh/ja the bare-vocative economy (贵族长/団長 still read as an office, not a nickname).

value.finding: Жилотдел is the stump-compound for жилищный отдел, the housing section of a local soviet executive committee (Russian Wiktionary: an institution for registering and allocating living space; marked colloquial). Under War Communism (1918-21) these offices seized 'surplus' housing and the furniture of requisitioned mansions and handed both out to new occupants on an ордер, a numbered official allocation order; the record-keeping was notoriously chaotic. In the novel (ch. V and XI) Vorobyaninov's furniture was carted 'в распоряжение жилотдела' in 1919; the office was disbanded in 1921 and its archive merged into Старкомхоз (the Stargorod municipal-economy department), whose archivist Korobeinikov keeps the chair orders at home; a settee is still in the office hall with grease on the cover, and 'Comrade Burkin, head of the housing department' handed one chair to Gritsatsuev. For a 1928 reader the word carried the flavour of the earliest, most arbitrary Soviet redistribution and of the ubiquitous NEP-era abbreviations the book mocks. The only English rendering verified in print is John Richardson's (1961) 'housing division' (Старкомхоз = 'the Stargorod communal services', ордер = 'order'). Chinese (Bai Huaxiong 2022, Shanghai Translation; earlier Zhang Peiwen 2004, Xu Changhan 1985) and Japanese (Egawa Taku 1969, Chikuma) editions exist but their wording for this term could not be checked online. The prompt's reference to Durov/VKontakte and 2013 is unrelated boilerplate and was disregarded.
value.note_for_reader: Housing Department (жилотдел): the local Soviet office that in 1918-21 confiscated 'surplus' rooms and furniture and reassigned them by written order; not to be confused with the municipal-economy department (коммунхоз) that absorbed it in 1921, or with a housing cooperative (жилтоварищество).
value.rationale: All three renderings keep the denotation (a government office allocating housing) and stay lexically distinct from коммунхоз (Municipal Services / 市政公用局 / 市公営事業局) and жилтоварищество (housing cooperative / 住房合作社 / 住宅組合), which the plot requires; 'Department' over Richardson's 'division' because it reads as an office with a head and an archive. What is given up is the clipped Soviet-acronym connotation (жил+отдел) and the War Communism menace the word carried in 1928; the one-line note restores the requisition context that the target reader cannot infer.

value.finding: Старкомхоз is a fictional Soviet-style syllabic acronym: Стар(городское) ком(мунальное) хоз(яйство), the Stargorod department of communal economy. In the 1920s the коммунальные отделы / комхозы of local soviets (formalised by the 8 April 1920 Sovnarkom decree, reorganised in 1923) ran housing, municipal land, благоустройство (street upkeep, kerbs, hoardings), water, sewerage, tramways and funeral services, under dual subordination to the executive committee and the NKVD; the comic point is that Gavrilin, 'transferred from Samarkand', chairs the body that must build the tram. In the text the family recurs: 'грузовики Старкомхоза', 'отдел благоустройства Старкомхоза', 'заведующий Старкомхозом Гаврилин', 'оркестр коммунальников', the 'клуб коммунальников' poster and the 'союз коммунальников', plus Ostap's toast 'за коммунальное хозяйство'. Richardson's 1961 English (lib.ru) uses 'the Stargorod communal services' throughout, with 'Communal Service Workers' Union/Club' and 'town-improvement department'; academic English (Klanderud 1995) simply transliterates 'Starkomkhoz'; Fisher's 2011 rendering could not be verified online. No Chinese (张佩文 1954/2004, 白桦熊) or Japanese (江川卓 1969) rendering of the term is retrievable online, so the zh/ja decisions rest on the meaning, not precedent. The brief's reference to 'Durov and VKontakte around 2013' does not apply to this term and was ignored.

rendering.en: the Stargorod Municipal Services (Starkomkhoz) on first mention, then 'Starkomkhoz' / 'the municipal services'; коммунальники = municipal-services workers; клуб коммунальников = Municipal Services Workers' Club; союз коммунальников = Municipal Services Workers' Union; отдел благоустройства = street-improvement department
rendering.zh: 斯塔尔戈罗德市政公用事业局（简称“市政公用局”）; коммунальники = 市政公用事业职工; клуб коммунальников = 市政公用事业职工俱乐部; союз коммунальников = 市政公用事业工会; отдел благоустройства = 市容整治科
rendering.ja: スタルゴロド市公共事業局（略称「市公共事業局」）; коммунальники = 公共事業労働者; клуб коммунальников = 公共事業労働者クラブ; союз коммунальников = 公共事業労組; отдел благоустройства = 街路整備課

value.note_for_reader: Starkomkhoz — Soviet-style acronym for the Stargorod 'communal economy' board: the city soviet's department for housing, utilities, trams and street upkeep, an institution for which 'communal' had no connotation of collective living.
value.rationale: Kept denotation (a city-soviet utilities-and-housing department) and the family unity of комхоз/коммунальники under one root ('municipal services' / 市政公用事业 / 公共事業), and kept the acronym flavour in English by retaining 'Starkomkhoz' after the first gloss; gave up the literal 'communal', which Richardson kept but which misleads an English reader toward kommunalki, and gave up the acronym itself in zh/ja, where transliterated Soviet acronyms carry nothing.

value.finding: The state almshouse in Stargorod, housed in Vorobyaninov's confiscated mansion: the sign in ch. VII reads '2-й дом социального обеспечения Старгубстраха', and the text then calls it '2-й дом Старсобеса', 'дом № 2 Старсобеса', '2-й дом собеса' (ch. VII, VIII, XI), while Tikhon (ch. V: 'У нас тут государственная богадельня: старухи живут на полном пенсионе') and the furniture trail (ch. IX: 'Это стул из богадельни') call it simply богадельня. Собес is the colloquial Soviet clipping of 'социальное обеспечение', the welfare office that paid pensions and ran homes for the old; Старсобес = Старгородский собес, a made-up acronym of the same type as the real губсобес/наркомсобес, and the joke is the 1920s habit of telescoping every institution into such syllable-strings, hung on what is really a pre-revolutionary almshouse full of old women in uniform. Its prototype, per Mikhail Shtikh's memoir, was a Moscow almshouse in Armyansky pereulok. In Russian usage the phrase is now a proverbial tag for petty embezzlement ('Завхоз 2-го дома Старсобеса был застенчивый ворюга'). Existing English translations do not keep the acronym: Richardson (1961) has 'the Second Home of Stargorod Social Security Administration' (and 'SECOND SOCIAL SECURITY HOME OF THE STAR-PROV-INS-AD' for the sign), Fisher (2011) 'the Second Stargorod Social Security Home'. I could not find online the wording used by the Chinese translators (张佩文 2004, 白桦熊 2022) or by 江川卓's Japanese version (1966/69), so zh and ja are decided on the same principle rather than on precedent.

rendering.zh: 斯塔尔戈罗德社保局第二养老院
rendering.ja: スタルゴロド社会保障局第二養老院

value.note_for_reader: Старсобес = Стар(городский) собес, the local Soviet welfare office (собес < социальное обеспечение); the 1920s mania for telescoping every institution into an acronym is the joke, and Tikhon and Ostap call the place what it is, a богадельня (almshouse).
value.rationale: All three keep the denotation (a state-run old people's home, numbered like any Soviet office, under the welfare department) and the deadpan bureaucratic register, and pair naturally with 'almshouse' / 养老院 / 養老院 for богадельня on the same pages; the acronym itself is given up in en and ja (following Richardson and Fisher, since the Russian column shows it and the note explains it), while zh keeps a trace of it through the natural Chinese clipping 社保. Dropped the parenthetical transliterations (Starsobes / 斯塔尔社保 / スタルソベス) as noise in a side-by-side edition.

value.finding: In the novel the institution is '2-й дом Старсобеса' (Старсобес = Старгородский собес, the Stargorod social-welfare office); the sign Ostap reads says 'СССР РСФСР / 2-й дом Старсобеса / Старгубстраха...' and the chapter 'Голубой воришка' opens 'Завхоз 2-го дома Старсобеса был застенчивый ворюга', then 'Он был не только завхозом, но и вообще заведующим' (Wikisource). Собес/соцобес is a colloquial Soviet-era clipping of 'социальное обеспечение' and also names the office that administers welfare (ru.wiktionary; Mokienko & Nikitina's Толковый словарь языка Совдепии cites exactly this passage under соцобес); the 'дом' is a state old-age home for pensioner women, whose real Moscow prototype was a former almshouse near Armyansky Lane (M. Shtikh's memoir, apotapov777). Завхоз = заведующий хозяйством, the supplies-and-premises manager, marked colloquial/special in Wiktionary; the joke is that this housekeeping post has swallowed the directorship, and Alkhen uses it to feed his relatives and sell the inventory. Established renderings: Richardson (1961) 'the Second Home of Stargorod Social Security Administration', sign 'SECOND SOCIAL SECURITY HOME OF THE STAR-PROV-INS-AD', завхоз = 'assistant warden' (which mistranslates the rank); Zhang Peiwen (人民文学出版社, 2004) '社会保障处第二院', завхоз = '总务主任', and his text glosses the place as '国家养老院'. Anne O. Fisher's 2011 rendering and Egawa Taku's Japanese (筑摩書房 1969) could not be checked directly; a Japanese reader's blog appears to use 社会保険局第二養老院 but the page did not load. Note: the brief's line about 'Durov and VKontakte' and 'around 2013' is a template artefact; the term belongs to 1927-28 Soviet NEP vocabulary.

rendering.en: the Second Social Security Home / the supply manager
rendering.zh: 社会保障处第二院 / 总务主任
rendering.ja: 社会保障局第二養老院 / 用度主任

value.note_for_reader: Собес: Soviet clipping of 'social security', also the welfare office itself; a завхоз runs an institution's supplies and premises, not the institution.
value.rationale: Keeps the denotation (a state welfare office's numbered old-age home; a housekeeping-and-supplies post below the director) and lets the 'not only supply manager but director' joke land; gives up the acronym texture of Старсобес and Richardson's 'assistant warden', which misstates the rank. Chinese follows Zhang Peiwen's established wording; Japanese has no verified precedent, so it uses transparent institutional terms.

value.finding: ЗАГС (отдел записи актов гражданского состояния) is the Soviet civil-registry office created by decree of 18 December 1917, which took the recording of births, marriages and deaths away from the churches; a 'делопроизводитель' was a low-grade office clerk who kept the files. In chapter I of the 1928 text Vorobyaninov 'служил в загсе, где ведал столом регистрации смертей и браков', and the narrator then calls him 'делопроизводитель загса' ('У делопроизводителя загса от злобы свалилось с носа пенснэ'); the discarded chapter published in 1929 is titled 'Прошлое регистратора ЗАГСа'. For a 1928 reader the joke is the fall from уездный предводитель дворянства to the pettiest of new Soviet paper-pushers, and the narrator's mock-official use of the full title as an epithet is what makes the pince-nez scene funny. John Richardson's standard English version renders it 'registry office' / 'the registry clerk'; English summaries of the book uniformly say 'registry office clerk'. The Egawa Taku Japanese translation (Shueisha 1966; Sekaiyūmoa bunko 1977) is not online, but Japanese coverage paraphrases the job as 登記所に勤める / 今は事務員; the Zhang Peiwen (人民文学 2004) and 上海译文 2022 Chinese texts are likewise not online, and Chinese summaries say 县登记处的工作人员, so the zh/ja wordings below are defensible rather than attested.
value.note_for_reader: ZAGS: the Soviet civil registry that recorded births, marriages and deaths, work the church had done before 1917.
value.rationale: All three keep the denotation (civil registry + lowly clerk) and the mock-official register that lets the full title serve as a jibe; 办事员/事務員 even carry the 'lowest grade' flavour. Given up: the acronym itself and the specifically Soviet novelty of a secular registry, which the one-line note supplies; 'record-keeper' or 'file clerk' was rejected because it loses the institution.

value.term: «Летопись войны 1914 года» / «Русский паломник» / «История раскола» / «Русский в Италии»
value.finding: Chapter III: Father Fyodor's wife has papered the inside of his small trunk with photographs cut from «Летопись войны 1914 года», and on top lie a bound set of «Русский паломник» for 1903, a very fat «История раскола» and a booklet «Русский в Италии» with a smoking Vesuvius on the cover. «Летопись войны 1914 года» is the real official illustrated weekly of the Great War (Petrograd, 1914-17, ed. Maj.-Gen. D. N. Dubensky, 132 issues; its title grew each year to «...1914-1917 гг.»), the pre-revolutionary tsarist-patriotic press par excellence. «Русский паломник» is the real pious illustrated weekly founded 1885 (A. I. Popovitsky, blessed by John of Kronstadt, published by P. P. Soikin), devoted to holy places, shrines and edifying tales. «История раскола» is a generic seminary-textbook title (Makary's «История русского раскола» and similar): раскол here means the 17th-century Old Believer schism after Patriarch Nikon's reforms, not a 'split' in general. The Italy booklet is a cheap tourist pamphlet and is not verifiable as a real title. Together the four items mark Father Fyodor as a provincial priest whose whole mental furniture is 1903-1914 tsarist piety and patriotism, now lying in mothballs beside twenty hidden gold coins. Existing English translations (Richardson 1961, echoed by Fisher 2011) give 'Chronicle of the 1914 War', 'Russian Pilgrim', 'History of the Schism', 'A Russian in Italy' (Richardson misdates the set 1913; the source says 1903). The published Chinese (张佩文 2004, 白桦熊, 徐昌翰 2022) and Japanese (江川卓 1961/1969) renderings of these titles could not be retrieved online, so zh/ja are settled by terminology rather than precedent.

rendering.en: The Chronicle of the War of 1914; The Russian Pilgrim; A History of the Schism; A Russian in Italy
rendering.zh: 《1914年战争纪事》《俄罗斯朝圣者》《教会分裂史》《俄国人在意大利》
rendering.ja: 『一九一四年戦争年代記』『ロシアの巡礼者』『教会分裂史』『イタリアのロシア人』

value.note_for_reader: Pre-1917 reading: an official illustrated weekly of the Great War, a pious pilgrimage magazine, and a seminary history of the 17th-century Old Believer schism (raskol).
value.rationale: Keeps denotation (translated titles, established English wording, 《》/『』 title punctuation) and the mock-solemn register of a catalogue of a priest's mothballed library; gives up the specific 'Old Believer' sense of раскол inside the titles, which would bloat them, and carries it in the one-line note instead.

value.finding: Ostap Bender's one stated biographical fact ('Мой папа был турецко-подданный', ch. 5), which the narrator then reuses as a mock-heraldic epithet. 'Турецко-подданный' is the Imperial legal term for an Ottoman subject; before 1917 many Odessa merchants, overwhelmingly Jews, bought cheap Ottoman papers to escape conscription (notably 1904), pogroms and Pale-of-Settlement residence limits, so to a 1928 reader the phrase was a wink meaning 'Odessa Jew' said in bureaucratic form, not a claim of Turkish blood; the Bender-bey / Ibragimovich / 'descendant of janissaries' jokes build on it. Soviet film casting later took it literally. English coverage is split: Richardson's 1961 translation and derived texts say 'Turkish citizen', while English Wikipedia and Fisher-era commentary use 'Turkish subject'. I could not retrieve the wording of the published Chinese (白桦熊 et al.) or Japanese (江川卓, 1966/1969) translations; a Japanese reader's summary paraphrases as 'トルコ人の血を引く'. The brief's mention of Durov/VKontakte/2013 is a template artefact and does not apply to this 1928 term.

rendering.en: the son of a Turkish subject

value.note_for_reader: Before 1917 many Odessa Jewish merchants took Ottoman (Turkish) subjecthood to escape conscription and residence restrictions; 'son of a Turkish subject' was a wink at such origins, phrased like a passport entry.
value.rationale: Keeps the denotation (a legal 'subject', not 'citizen', matching the pre-revolutionary term 臣民/subject in all three languages) and the stiff official register that makes the epithet funny on repetition; gives up the connotation of Jewish Odessa origin, which no rendering can carry and which the one-line note supplies.

value.finding: In 1920s Soviet usage a концессионер was a foreign firm or capitalist granted a концессия (concession) under Lenin's decree of 23 Nov 1920: a state-licensed right to exploit Soviet resources or run an enterprise for profit, negotiated through Главконцесском (1923–30); concessions peaked at 103 in 1926 and were being wound down as the novel appeared, so the word was live NEP business-page jargon. In chapter VI Bender fixes the joke himself: 'как непосредственный участник концессии и технический руководитель дела, получаю шестьдесят процентов', and from then on the narrator calls the pair 'концессионеры' as a fixed, deadpan collective noun (some 20 occurrences in the 1928 text: 'концессионеры побывали в Старкомхозе', 'Все головы повернулись в сторону концессионеров', 'Разговаривая подобным образом, концессионеры приткнулись к чебоксарскому берегу'). Shcheglov's commentary treats the label as a mock-official narrative formula in the classic-picaresque manner but does not gloss the term itself. Both published English versions (Richardson 1961, Fisher 2011) keep 'the concessionaires' throughout. I could not open the Chinese (张佩文 2004 and others) or Japanese (江川卓 1969) texts online, so their renderings are not verified.
value.note_for_reader: Концессия/'concession' was the NEP-era licence letting foreign capitalists run a Soviet enterprise for a cut; the narrator mock-solemnly grants the two treasure-hunters the title.
value.rationale: All three keep the denotation (holder of a state concession) and the dry official register, and are used as one fixed word every time; zh 租让者 is the term of Chinese Lenin/NEP historiography rather than the modern franchise word 特许经营者, and ja 利権者 uses the period word for Soviet concessions (北樺太石油利権) instead of the pejorative 利権屋, giving up some immediate transparency in zh and ja, which the one-line note restores.

value.finding: Отец Фёдор is Fyodor Ivanovich Vostrikov, parish priest of the Church of Frol and Lavr in the provincial town N, who hears Madame Petukhova's deathbed confession about the jewels and abandons his parish to hunt the chairs in rivalry with Bender and Vorobyaninov; he ends up broke and in a psychiatric ward after a chase to the Caucasus. 'Отец' here is the ordinary Orthodox address for a priest (батюшка), not kinship; the comedy is that a man of the cloth, a seminary dropout who took orders to dodge the 1915 draft, is a greedy failed entrepreneur (rabbits, marble soap, the dream of a 'candle factory in Samara'), so for a Russian reader the title carries mock-solemn irony against his mercenary behaviour. Existing renderings are settled: English translations and film coverage use 'Father Fyodor'; the standard Chinese translation (张佩文, 人民文学出版社 2004) and its blurbs call him 神父费多尔 / 费多尔神父; the Japanese translation by 江川卓 (集英社/筑摩書房) is cited as フョードル神父. The prompt's stray reference to Durov and VKontakte does not apply to this term and was ignored.
value.rationale: All three keep the clerical title (Father / 神父 / 神父) so the mock-solemn contrast with his greed survives, and follow the renderings already established in the English, Zhang Peiwen Chinese and Ekawa Japanese translations; zh binds 费多尔 rather than the fuller transliteration 费奥多尔 to match that edition, giving up nothing of denotation. What is lost is the specifically Orthodox flavour of 'батюшка/отец' (神父 in zh/ja reads as generic or Catholic), which is not worth a note.

value.finding: Ippolit Matveyevich Vorobyaninov, nicknamed Kisa ('Kitty', his childhood pet name that Ostap Bender adopts), is the co-protagonist of The Twelve Chairs: born 1875, uyezd marshal of the nobility from 1912, a gambler and provincial scandal before 1917, and after the revolution a clerk at the ZAGS civil registry in the town of N. For a Russian reader he is a proverbial figure, 'the giant of thought, father of Russian democracy', a pompous, helpless relic of the old order, so beloved that statues of him stand in Pyatigorsk (2008) and Kharkiv (2009). English coverage and both major translations (Richardson 1961, Fisher 2011) spell him Ippolit Matveyevich Vorobyaninov. Chinese translations (Zhang Peiwen, People's Literature 2004; Xu Changhan, Jiangsu Phoenix 2022; Bai Huaxiong, Shanghai Translation 2022) consistently use the surname 沃洛比亚尼诺夫, not 沃罗比亚尼诺夫; Egawa Takashi's Japanese translation (Shueisha 1966, reissued 1969/1977) writes イポリット・マトベイッチ・ボロビヤニノフ, while current Japanese web usage prefers ヴォロビヤニノフ.

rendering.ja: イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ・ヴォロビヤニノフ

The connotation of the patronymic as respectful address, and the comic contrast with 'Kisa', cannot be carried by the name itself and is given to the one-line note.

value.finding: Ostap Bender's refrain, first spoken in Chapter VI when he takes charge of the chair hunt ('Спокойно, спокойно. За дело берусь я. Заседание продолжается') and repeated in Chapters IX–XI and beyond; the reference site dslov.ru lists it as one of the novel's proverbial 'Benderisms' meaning 'the business goes on / back to work'. It is not a committee 'meeting': it is paired with Bender's other courtroom refrain 'Лед тронулся, господа присяжные заседатели!' ('gentlemen of the jury'), so заседание here is a court session and the joke is a swindler chairing his own trial in mock-judicial tones. Established renderings follow that courtroom sense: English-language coverage (Wikipedia/TV Tropes, and the 1961 Richardson tradition) gives 'The hearing is continued!'; the 2022 Chinese edition and its Douban editor's note give the catchphrase as '庭审继续进行！'. No online Japanese rendering could be found (Egawa Taku's 1966/1969 translation is not online), so the ja choice below is my own. The brief's mention of Durov/VKontakte and 2013 appears to be a template error; the term has no connection to them.
value.note_for_reader: Bender's mock-courtroom refrain, twin to 'The ice has broken, gentlemen of the jury!'; now a Russian proverb for 'back to business'.
value.rationale: Kept the courtroom denotation and the mock-solemn register that make the joke, and adopted the established en/zh renderings; gave up the neutral 'meeting/session' proposals (which lose the jury pairing) and, for ja, an attested rendering, since none was found. Bind 陪審員諸君/陪审员先生们/gentlemen of the jury consistently alongside it, and keep 'маленькое совещание' as an ordinary 'little conference'/小会/ちょっとした協議, distinct from this refrain.

value.term: «Зерцало грешного» / лубок / «Сим молитву деет, Хам пшеницу сеет, Яфет власть имеет. Смерть всем владеет»
value.finding: «Зерцало грешного» ('Mirror of the Sinner', title spelt «Зерцало грешнаго» on the sheets) is a real 18th-century Russian moralising lubok (popular print, engraved on copper and hand-coloured), known in many versions from Peter the Great's era; the Russian National Library holds a Moscow sheet dated 1741 and the State Historical Museum copies from 1820-1840. Odessky and Feldman's commentary, citing Rovinsky's 'Русские народные картинки' (vols 3 and 5), describe its four upper scenes captioned with the Church-Slavonic quatrain about Noah's sons (Shem prays, Ham sows, Japheth rules, Death owns all) and a foldable sheet that turns a fashionable couple into Death with a scythe and a sinner in hellfire; the same quatrain resurfaces in Tynyanov's 'Восковая персона' (1931). In the novel it hangs in Father Fyodor's room and 'consoles' him after his rabbit-breeding scheme fails: the joke is the priest drawing memento-mori comfort from a cheap old print while plotting to grab the jewels. Existing renderings: Richardson (1961) 'The Parable of the Sinner' with 'Shem saith a prayer, Ham soweth wheat, Japheth enjoyeth power, Death overtaketh all' and 'folk-painting'; Fisher (Northwestern UP, 2011) 'The Sinner's Mirror'; Chinese editions give ch. 3 as 罪人警鉴 (quatrain 闪在祷告，含在种麦，雅弗掌权。死神主宰一切) and, in Xu Changhan's 2022 version, 劝世图; no Japanese chapter title could be verified (Egawa Taku's 1969 translation is not online).

rendering.en: 'The Sinner's Mirror' (a lubok, a hand-coloured folk print): 'Shem doth pray, Ham soweth wheat, Japheth holdeth sway. Death ruleth all'
rendering.zh: 《罪人警鉴》（民间版画“卢博克”）：“闪祈祷，含播麦，雅弗掌权。死神统御万物”
rendering.ja: 『罪人の鏡』（民衆版画ルボーク）：「セムは祈り、ハムは麦を播き、ヤペテは権を執る。死は万物を統べる」

value.note_for_reader: A lubok is a cheap Russian popular print (woodcut or copperplate, hand-coloured), sold at fairs from the 1600s to 1917; this one, an 18th-century memento mori, shows Noah's sons at their stations in life and Death above them all.
value.rationale: Kept the denotation (a named, real print), the mock-solemn archaic register (English -eth forms, Chinese 警鉴 and four-beat lines, Japanese 執る/統べる) and Fisher's established English title; gave up the rhyme of the Slavonic original and, in Japanese, any established title, since none could be verified.

value.finding: A fictional NEP-era bakers' cooperative (артель) in Stargorod, chapter 10: its azure sign reads ОДЕССКАЯ БУБЛИЧНАЯ АРТЕЛЬ / МОСКОВСКИЕ БАРАНКИ, with a smirking young man pouring 'ochre Moscow baranki, passed off as needed as Odessa bubliki' from a cornucopia; its chairman Kislyarsky is the timid merchant conscripted into the 'Union of the Sword and Ploughshare' and later fleeced again in the Caucasus, muttering about 'stagnation in the baranka-and-bublik trade'. The joke is a provincial firm advertising two rival regional brands at once and selling one ring as the other: a bublik is the large soft yeast ring (boiled then baked, the southern/Odessa bagel), a baranka the small hard dry ring of central Russia; a 'Moscow' variety never existed and the phrase 'московские баранки' entered Russian mainly from this book. Richardson's 1961 English has 'Odessa Roll Bakery / Moscow Bun Artel', which drops the ring-bread pairing; Fisher's 2011 version and the published Chinese (白桦熊, 张佩文) and Japanese (江川卓, 1969) renderings could not be checked online. The prompt's references to Durov/VKontakte and 2013 do not apply to this 1928 term.

value.note_for_reader: Bublik: a big soft ring like a bagel, an Odessa speciality; baranka: a small hard dry Moscow tea-ring. The sign sells both cities at once.
value.rationale: Kept the denotation (a cooperative bakery, two distinct ring breads, the Odessa/Moscow clash) and the mock-solemn signboard register by rendering bublik with the familiar bagel and leaving 'Moscow Baranki' as a brand name in quotes; gave up self-explanatory baranki, hence the one-line note, and did not adopt Richardson's roll/bun pair, which loses the joke.

value.finding: Жилтоварищество is the NEP-era contraction of жилищное товарищество, the tenants' housing partnership created by the 1921–22 decrees and formalised in 1924 as the ЖАКТ (жилищно-арендное кооперативное товарищество): the residents of a municipalised house formed a cooperative that leased the building from the local Soviet, elected a board, collected rent, did repairs and allotted rooms among its members. By 1924–26 most Moscow and Leningrad housing was run this way, so for a 1928 reader the word meant ordinary self-managed tenant democracy, with its meetings, boards and squabbles over square metres; it was abolished in 1937. In chapter XVI the expelled 'ex-chemists' have turned the pink hostel into 'нечто среднее между жилтовариществом и феодальным поселком' — the joke sets a legal, collective, cooperative form of house government against a feudal fief held by force. Richardson's canonical English translation (lib.ru text) renders the pair 'something between a housing co-operative and a feudal settlement'. The prompt's mention of 'Durov and VKontakte' and 'around 2013' does not apply to this 1928 term; no Chinese or Japanese rendering of this specific sentence was found online, so those bindings rest on the standard terms for a housing cooperative.
value.note_for_reader: жилтоварищество: a 1920s tenants' cooperative that leased a house from the city and ran it by elected board — self-government, as opposed to the feudal fief the ex-chemists actually hold.
value.rationale: Keeps the denotation (a tenants' cooperative, i.e. a form of collective governance, so the contrast with 'feudal settlement' still reads as two political orders) and the dry bureaucratic register, following Richardson's established English; gives up the clipped Soviet-acronym flavour of the portmanteau and the specifically NEP-era legal status, which the note supplies.

value.finding: Polesov is a fictional Stargorod character in chapters X and XIV: a self-employed слесарь with his own motor-repair workshop (second yard of 7 Pereleshinsky Lane) who is never found in it, botches every order from the municipal housing office, and hangs about every street incident giving orders; the authors tag him 'слесарь-интеллигент', 'кустарь-одиночка с мотором' and 'кипучий лентяй' ('Он постоянно пенился'). The tag 'слесарь-интеллигент' was a deliberate NEP-era joke: 'интеллигент' was then a semi-pejorative class label, so a manual craftsman styling himself one is the mock-solemn point; a 2013 reader still uses 'слесарь-интеллигент' and 'кипучий лентяй' as proverbial labels for a fussy, self-important bungler. In chapter XIV Ostap, staging the fake monarchist 'Союз меча и орала', praises him: 'Браво, гусар! ... Для гусара-одиночки с мотором этого на первый раз достаточно.' John Richardson's standard English translation (lib.ru text) renders him 'Victor Mikhailovich Polesov, the mechanic-intellectual', keeps 'artisans owning cars' for кустари с мотором, 'ebullient idler' for кипучий лентяй and 'Well done, hussar ... a car-owning hussar working by himself'; Anne O. Fisher's 2011 retranslation also uses the name unchanged. The Chinese edition (张佩文 译, 人民文学出版社, 2004) titles chapter 10 '钳工、鹦鹉和女巫', establishing 钳工 (fitter/metalworker) rather than 水管工 (plumber) for слесарь; the Japanese translation (江川卓 訳, 集英社 1966/1977) exists but its rendering of the name was not verifiable online, so ポレソフ follows standard katakana practice.

rendering.ja: ヴィクトル・ミハイロヴィチ・ポレソフ

value.note_for_reader: Polesov, a self-employed metalworker with a motor-repair shed; the authors' tag 'locksmith-intellectual' mocks a craftsman posing as a member of the intelligentsia. Bind his tag as en 'the mechanic-intellectual' (Richardson's precedent; he repairs engines), zh '钳工知识分子' (钳工, not 水管工), ja 'インテリ鍛冶屋・機械工'; Ostap's 'гусар' as 'hussar' / '骠骑兵' / '軽騎兵'.
value.rationale: The name is a plain transliteration in all three languages, matching existing English and Chinese editions, so denotation and neutral register are kept; the connotation lives in the recurring epithets, which are bound in the note so that 'слесарь' is not flattened to 'plumber' and the mock-solemn 'intellectual' pairing survives, at the cost of the period-specific class sting of 'интеллигент' that no target language carries.

value.finding: Title of an unpainted 'brilliantly conceived' picture that Ostap Bender, in the Stargorod caretaker's room (ch. 5, «Великий комбинатор»), thinks of peddling to the children's commission for about 400 roubles; the text itself adds that it is modelled on Repin's popular «Запорожцы пишут письмо султану» (1880–91, standard English title 'Reply of the Zaporozhian Cossacks'; the Cossacks composing an obscene defiant reply to the Ottoman sultan). Chamberlain is Sir Austen Chamberlain, British Foreign Secretary, whose note of 23 Feb 1927 demanded that the USSR stop anti-British propaganda and aid to the Kuomintang; the Soviet press answered with the mass campaign «Наш ответ Чемберлену» (Pravda 27 Feb 1927; an Osoaviakhim aviation fund of that name from June 1927; squadrons and tank columns so named), and Britain broke off relations in May 1927. The phrase «наш ответ Чемберлену» became and remains a proverbial Russian idiom for a defiant tit-for-tat retort, which a 2013 reader still catches instantly; the joke is that Ostap is monetising the loudest propaganda meme of 1927 with a hack Repin pastiche. Ilf and Petrov were also echoing a real genre: «Красный перец» (1923) ran the cartoon 'Большевики пишут ответ английскому Керзону' and «Крокодил» (1927) 'Рабочие пишут ответ Чемберлену', both restaging Repin's canvas with Soviet figures. Existing English versions: Richardson (1961) 'The Bolsheviks Answer Chamberlain' / 'The Zaporozhe Cossacks Answer the Sultan'; Fisher (Northwestern, 2011) 'The Bolsheviks Writing a Letter to Chamberlain' / 'The Zaporozhian Cossacks Writing a Letter to the Turkish Sultan'. No Chinese or Japanese rendering of the painting title surfaced online (the 江川卓 Japanese and Chinese editions are not searchable), but Repin's picture has fixed titles in both languages: 《查波罗什人给土耳其苏丹写信》 and 『トルコのスルタンへ手紙を書くザポロージャ・コサック』, and Chamberlain is 张伯伦 / チェンバレン.
sources: http://gemeinwohl.jp/2019/05/08/イリヤ・レーピンの『トルコのスルタンへ手紙を/
https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/オースティン・チェンバレン

rendering.ja: 『チェンバレンへ手紙を書くボリシェヴィキ』

value.note_for_reader: Austen Chamberlain, British Foreign Secretary, sent the USSR a hostile note in Feb. 1927; the Soviet press's slogan «Наш ответ Чемберлену» ('Our answer to Chamberlain') was the propaganda catchphrase of the year and is still proverbial. Ostap's title recasts Repin's famous canvas (in the same sentence) as that answer.
value.rationale: Kept denotation and the mock-solemn exhibition-catalogue register by translating the title literally and in each language echoing the established title of Repin's painting (Fisher's English wording, and the 写信 / 手紙を書く pattern of the standard zh/ja Repin titles) so the pastiche is visible; the 1927 topicality and the idiom «наш ответ Чемберлену» cannot be carried in a title and are given to a one-line note. Richardson's 'Answer Chamberlain' was set aside because it drops the literal 'writing a letter' link that the Russian sentence itself relies on.

value.finding: In chapter I of The Twelve Chairs (1928) this is the broad main street of the county town N where Vorobyaninov lives, lined by the coffin shops of the 'Nymph' bureau and Bezenchuk; it recurs later (Gos. No. 1 stuck at the corner of Staropanskaya Square and this street; Bender and Vorobyaninov come out onto it). The Odessky–Feldman commentary explains the joke: the typical main street of a provincial town was 'Gubernatorskaya' (Governor's Street), and the Soviet renaming 'named after Comrade Gubernsky' changes the sound but not the substance — a deadpan jab at the 1920s wave of renaming streets after party figures ('gubernsky' also means simply 'provincial'). A real ulitsa Gubernskogo exists in Novorossiysk (formerly Tsemesskaya; renamed for A. Yu. Gubernsky, shot by the Whites in 1918), and some scholars think Ilf and Petrov, who visited the city, borrowed it; the name is not a well-known person, so for the 1928 reader it read as a generic obscure local hero. Both English translations (Richardson 1961, Fisher 2011) render it 'Comrade Gubernsky Street'; Zhang Peiwen's Chinese (People's Literature, 2004) has '名为古别伦斯基同志的大街'. No text of Egawa Takashi's Japanese translation is online, so the Japanese rendering is unverified. The prompt's reference to 'Durov and VKontakte, around 2013' does not apply to this term and was ignored.

value.finding: Беспризорные (lit. 'unsupervised', 'uncared-for'; also беспризорники) were the orphaned and abandoned children of the World War, revolution, civil war and the 1921-22 Volga famine: estimates run to 4.5-7 million by 1921-22, falling to about 250,000 by 1926 after Dzerzhinsky's Children's Commission (Деткомиссия, 27 Jan 1921), mass round-ups (from April 1928) and orphanages and labour communes; a 1935 decree declared the phenomenon eliminated. They lived by begging, petty theft, peddling and prostitution, rode the rails, formed gangs with their own argot, and in cities slept in cellars and in the still-warm cauldrons used for boiling road asphalt, which is exactly the image in ch. XVI: 'Беспризорные сидели возле асфальтового чана и с наслаждением вдыхали запах кипящей смолы'. For a 1928 reader the word was a fixture of daily street life and of newspaper campaigns, not a euphemism: pitied and feared at once, a stock target of charity appeals (Ostap's fake 'Children's Aid' collection later in the book trades on this). English scholarship keeps the Russian word (besprizornye/besprizorniki) or says 'homeless children'; Richardson's 1961 translation uses 'waifs', en.wikipedia uses 'street children', 'waifs', 'urchins'. Chinese historical writing (e.g. the translation of Goldman's Women, the State and Revolution) uses 流浪儿童, while Chinese reviews of the novel say 流浪儿. Japanese coverage transliterates ベスプリゾルニキ with the gloss 家のない子どもたち, and Japanese writing on Makarenko's 1920s colonies uses 浮浪児.
value.note_for_reader: беспризорные: the millions of orphaned street children left by war, revolution and famine, a fixture of 1920s Soviet cities; they slept in cellars and in warm asphalt cauldrons.
value.rationale: All three renderings keep the denotation (unsupervised street children, not adults) and the period flavour: 'waifs' is Richardson's established word and carries the pity-plus-menace connotation, 流浪儿 is the wording Chinese readers of the novel already use, and 浮浪児 is the Japanese word for exactly this post-war phenomenon (Japan's own 1945 浮浪児), so it lands without explanation. Given up: the specifically Soviet scale and the state-campaign resonance of the word, which the one-line note restores; the Russian word itself is not carried, since a transliteration would mean nothing to this reader.

value.finding: Klavdia Ivanovna Petukhova is Vorobyaninov's mother-in-law in Ilf and Petrov's The Twelve Chairs: a pre-revolutionary provincial gentlewoman living with him in Stargorod, who on 15 April 1927 has a bad dream, suffers a stroke, and on her deathbed confesses to him and to Father Fyodor that she sewed her jewels into one of the twelve Gambs dining chairs. The chapter title 'Кончина мадам Петуховой' pairs the solemn 'кончина' with the pre-revolutionary, faintly bourgeois 'мадам', mock-obituary style, for a woman the narrator otherwise calls 'старуха' and 'теща' and whom her son-in-law openly dislikes. Existing renderings: John Richardson's English (1961, the standard one) uses 'Claudia Ivanovna', 'Madame Petukhov's Demise', 'the old woman', 'his mother-in-law'; Chinese: 张佩文 (人民文学 名著名译) uses 克拉芙季娅·伊万诺夫娜, chapter '别图霍娃夫人谢世', 岳母, 老太婆; 徐昌翰 (江苏凤凰文艺 2022) uses 佩图霍娃 ('佩图霍娃魂归地府'). Japanese: the only translation is 江川卓's 十二の椅子 (集英社 1966 / 筑摩 1969 / 世界ユーモア文庫 1977); no page found quoting its rendering of her name, so the Japanese form is by transliteration rule, not attested.

value.note_for_reader: 'Madame' in the chapter title is the narrator's mock-genteel, pre-revolutionary courtesy title for a woman the text otherwise calls 'the old woman' and 'his mother-in-law'.
value.rationale: Binds the name to three fixed forms that must stay distinct throughout: name-and-patronymic (Klavdia Ivanovna / 克拉夫季娅·伊万诺夫娜 / クラヴディヤ・イワーノヴナ) for the narrator's neutral voice, 'Madame Petukhova' / 彼图霍娃夫人 / マダム・ペトゥホワ only where the source has 'мадам Петухова' (the chapter title's mock obituary), and 'his mother-in-law' / 岳母 / 姑 (義母) plus 'the old woman' / 老太婆 / 老婆 for 'теща' and 'старуха'. Kept denotation and the ironic register; gave up Richardson's anglicised 'Claudia' and 'Petukhov' (feminine surname kept so the side-by-side reader can match the Russian) and, in Chinese, standardised 张佩文's 别图霍娃 / 徐昌翰's 佩图霍娃 to the modern standard 彼图霍娃; Japanese マダム rather than 夫人 keeps the faintly bourgeois, comic tint of 'мадам'.

value.finding: «Прага» is the famous restaurant at Arbat 2, Moscow, made grand by the merchant Tararykin from the 1890s and, per Gilyarovsky, the best-appointed restaurant in the city. After nationalisation it reopened on 15 Oct 1924 as a public 'образцовая (образцово-показательная) столовая' of the Moscow consumer cooperative (sources name Моссельпром or МСПО; Mayakovsky's jingle ran «В столовой Моссельпрома — бывшая Прага»), keeping mirrors, flowers and an evening orchestra, i.e. a restaurant in all but name. МСПО = Московский союз потребительских обществ, the Moscow consumer co-op union (founded 1898; its national successor was Центросоюз). Shcheglov's commentary notes that in 1927 even Moscow's most representative restaurants were officially called столовые, so the joke is the officialese label 'model canteen' on a place where Vorobyaninov's bill comes to 9 r. 20 k. and Liza, who has never seen a 'large model restaurant', is dazzled. Richardson (1961) renders it 'the Prague Restaurant, the showpiece of the Moscow union of consumer societies'; Fisher's 2011 wording and the Chinese (张佩文, 徐昌翰, 白桦熊) and Japanese (江川卓) renderings were not accessible online. Japanese sources give Центросоюз as 消費者協同組合中央同盟 / ツェントロソユーズ; Wikidata's Chinese label is 苏联消费合作社.

rendering.en: the Prague, model canteen of the Moscow Consumer Co-op (MSPO)
rendering.zh: “布拉格”——莫斯科消费合作社联社（MSPO）的示范食堂
rendering.ja: モスクワ消費組合連合（MSPO）の模範食堂「プラーガ」

value.note_for_reader: In NEP Moscow even the grandest restaurants were officially 'canteens' of a state or co-op body; the Prague, pre-1917 the city's most luxurious, was one such 'model canteen'.
value.rationale: Keeps the denotation (the real Arbat restaurant, the co-op that ran it) and the ironic register of officialese 'model canteen / 示范食堂 / 模範食堂' set against a mirrored restaurant with a nine-ruble bill; gives up Richardson's smoother 'showpiece' and the expansion of МСПО beyond a short one-word-ish gloss, which the acronym in parentheses carries for cross-language matching.

value.finding: Ostap Bender is the fictional con-man protagonist of Ilf and Petrov's The Twelve Chairs (1928) and The Little Golden Calf (1931), self-styled Ostap-Suleyman-Berta-Maria-Bender-Bey, 'son of a Turkish subject' from Odessa; his surname is the Bessarabian town Bender/Bendery, and his epithet 'великий комбинатор' (the great schemer) became a Russian catchphrase. For a Russian reader of the 2010s the name is proverbial: 'Остап Бендер' or 'Бендер' means a charming, resourceful swindler who works '400 relatively honest ways' inside the letter of the law, and post-Soviet culture has half-rehabilitated him as an entrepreneur figure with statues in several cities. Every English translation (Richardson 1961, Fisher/Northwestern 2012) uses 'Ostap Bender'. Japanese editions (江川卓, Shueisha 1966/1969) and reference works (コトバンク) use オスタップ・ベンデル. Chinese usage is split: the older 徐昌翰 translation (春风文艺 1985, reissued 江苏凤凰文艺 2022) writes 奥斯塔普·本杰尔, while the newest translation (白桦熊, 上海译文 2021) and the CJK reference form use 奥斯塔普·本德尔; the latter matches the standard Xinhua transliteration of 'Бендер'. Note: the prompt's reference to Durov/VKontakte is unrelated to this term and was ignored.

rendering.ja: オスタップ・ベンデル

value.note_for_reader: Ostap Bender, the novel's 'great schemer', became a Russian byword for a charming swindler; 'Comrade Bender' is the standard Soviet form of address, and the newspaper notice's abbreviated 'т. Бендер' is kept abbreviated in English as 'Cde. Bender' (Chinese 本德尔同志 and Japanese ベンデル同志 have no printed abbreviation).
value.rationale: Denotation and register are kept exactly by binding the one transliteration each language's published translations already use (en unanimous; ja unanimous; zh the modern standard 本德尔 over the older 本杰尔); the connotation 'proverbial con man' cannot be carried by a name and is left to the narrative and a one-line note. For 'т. Бендер' use the abbreviated 'Cde. Bender' in English; Chinese and Japanese have no abbreviation for 同志, so keep 本德尔同志 / ベンデル同志 unabbreviated.

value.finding: ГПУ (Государственное политическое управление) was the Soviet secret police of the RSFSR, created on 6 February 1922 by VTsIK decree as the direct successor of the Cheka and placed inside the NKVD; on 15 November 1923 it became the all-Union ОГПУ under Sovnarkom. Despite the renaming, the short form 'ГПУ' stayed in the names of local organs and in everyday speech and literature (Bulgakov, Ilf and Petrov, Olesha, Mandelstam) through the 1920s-30s, so for a 1928 reader it simply meant 'the secret police', with the Cheka's menace still attached. In the novel the term is punchline material: Bender's 'Вам некуда торопиться. ГПУ к вам само придёт' (ch. 14, the 'Sword and Ploughshare' scene) became a proverb, and Russian sites still quote it as such. English coverage (Wikipedia, Fisher's translation apparatus) uses 'GPU' / 'State Political Directorate'; Chinese uses 国家政治保卫局 with the transliteration 格别乌; Japanese uses ゲーペーウー with 国家政治保安部 (or 国家政治局). The prompt's mention of 2013, Durov and VKontakte does not fit this term and was ignored; the research concerns the 1922-1928 institution.

rendering.en: the GPU (the secret police) — first occurrence; thereafter 'the GPU'
rendering.zh: 国家政治保卫局（格别乌，秘密警察）——首次出现；此后用“格别乌”
rendering.ja: ゲーペーウー（国家政治保安部、秘密警察）――初出のみ；以後は「ゲーペーウー」

value.note_for_reader: GPU: the Soviet secret police of the 1920s, successor to the Cheka and forerunner of the NKVD/KGB; renamed OGPU in 1923 but still called 'GPU' in speech.
value.rationale: Keeps denotation (an expanded gloss on first use in each language, using the established Wikipedia-level names) and register (the characters' flat, matter-of-fact acronym, which is what makes Bender's joke land), while giving up the automatic chill a 1928 reader felt at the letters; the one-line note supplies that instead of a footnote at every occurrence.

value.finding: Both are real pre-revolutionary charities, named here in Chapter XIX («Баллотировка по-европейски»), where the 'Union of the Sword and Ploughshare' conspirators hand out the offices of a restored old regime and «Елену Станиславовну выбрали попечительницей обществ «Капля молока» и «Белый цветок»». «Капля молока» (a calque of the French 'Goutte de lait', Fécamp 1891) was the name of infant-welfare stations that gave sterilised milk and doctor's consultations to poor mothers; the first Russian ones opened in St Petersburg and Odessa in 1901, and towns such as Arkhangelsk followed (1910). «Белый цветок» / «День белой ромашки» was the anti-tuberculosis flower day of the All-Russian League against Tuberculosis, first held 20 April 1911, in which society ladies and students sold paper daisies and the imperial family ran bazaars in Yalta; it stopped after 1917. For a 1928 reader the pair evoked the genteel, ladies'-committee philanthropy of the tsarist provincial town, so making the ex-mistress and fortune-teller Elena Stanislavovna its 'patroness' is a joke about the conspirators' fantasy of restored respectability. Existing English, Chinese and Japanese renderings of this line (Richardson, Fisher, the Chinese and Egawa Japanese editions) could not be retrieved online; the literal society names are the only established form.

rendering.en: the 'Drop of Milk' and 'White Flower' charitable societies
rendering.ja: 「一滴のミルク」と「白い花」の両慈善協会

value.note_for_reader: Real tsarist-era charities: 'Drop of Milk' stations gave sterilised milk to poor infants; 'White Flower' was the anti-tuberculosis flower-day society (from 1911) patronised by society ladies and the imperial family.
value.rationale: Kept the denotation (literal, quoted society names, as in the source) and the mock-solemn register of the office list; added one word, 'charitable' (慈善/慈善), so the trilingual reader knows these are ladies' charities and gets the joke without a footnote, giving up the instant period colour a 1928 Russian reader had.

value.finding: Допр (ДОПР) is a 1920s Soviet penal acronym; its expansion is itself contested: the Dictionary of the Language of Sovdepia and Russian Wikipedia give 'дом принудительных работ' / 'дом общественно-принудительных работ' (house of compulsory labour, one of the 'general places of confinement' of 1918–1922, transferred to the NKVD in 1923 and especially common in the Ukrainian SSR, e.g. Kharkiv and Stalino), while commentaries on the novel gloss it as 'дом предварительного заключения' (pre-trial detention house). In practice a допр held both remand prisoners and short-term convicts, so for a 1928 reader it meant simply 'the local jail', with a NEP-era flavour: Kislyarsky's 'допровская корзинка' in ch. 27 is the NEPman's ever-packed prison basket. In ch. VIII Ostap threatens Pasha Emilievich: 'Один мой знакомый тоже продавал государственную мебель. Теперь он пошел в монахи — сидит в допре' — 'went into a monastery' is a cell joke, and the punchline only lands if допр is plainly a jail. Anne O. Fisher's 2011 translation (Northwestern) renders it 'He's doing time in the lockup' (p. 100) and uses 'lockup' again for Kislyarsky's basket (p. 411); Richardson's 1961 abridgement has no trace of the line (search-within finds no monk/lockup passage there) and uses 'jail' for the basket chapter. No published Chinese or Japanese rendering of this line could be located online.
value.rationale: Keeps denotation (a jail, not a labour camp) and the offhand colloquial register so the 'became a monk' joke stays plain; gives up the period acronym and its specifically Soviet/Ukrainian institutional connotation. 'The lockup' is Fisher's established English; 看守所 and 拘置所 are the everyday modern words for a pre-trial jail in Chinese and Japanese, instantly clear without a note.
