value.finding: First line and title of Afanasy Fet's 1842 poem, set the same year by Alexander Varlamov as a drawing-room romance (first sung by the tenor Bantyshev); by 1850 the critic Apollon Grigoriev already called it 'almost a folk song', and it remained a standard of the Russian romance repertoire (Lemeshev, Viktoria Ivanova, Pogudin) into the 2010s, so a Russian reader of 2013 heard it instantly as a sentimental old song. In Chapter XIV Ostap uses it as mock-tender cover for stealing the chair from his sleeping bride, the widow Gritsatsueva, before leaving the note 'Going to Novokhopersk with a report. Don't wait for me at dinner. Your Suslik.' The joke is the gap between the languid parlour lyric and the burglary it excuses. The standard English translation (John Richardson, 1961) renders it as the bare quotation 'Don't wake her at dawn!' with no attribution; the romance itself is sold in English as 'Do not wake her at dawn'. No established Chinese or Japanese title for the poem or romance surfaced in search (a Japanese art-song index lists the poem only under an ad-hoc gloss), and no rendering from the Chinese (费明君, 安郁琛/钟鼎, 白桦熊) or Japanese (江川卓) translations of the novel could be retrieved.

rendering.zh: 《黎明时莫将她唤醒》（费特的浪漫曲）
rendering.ja: 「暁に彼女を起こすな」（フェートのロマンス）

value.note_for_reader: Opening line of Fet's 1842 poem, set by Varlamov as one of the best-known Russian drawing-room romances.
value.rationale: Keeps the denotation and the quotation-marking (quotes plus a two-word source tag, so the reader knows Ostap is singing, not confessing) and the mock-tender register in all three languages; gives up the instant recognition a Russian reader had, which the one-line note restores, and in zh/ja gives up an established title because none exists to prefer.

value.finding: In the Russian text (az.lib.ru) 'концессия' and 'концессионеры' occur about 68 times and 'компаньоны' about 19: Ostap frames the treasure hunt as a 'концессия' from the first bargaining scene ('как непосредственный участник концессии и технический руководитель дела, получаю шестьдесят процентов'), and the narrator then mock-solemnly calls the pair 'концессионеры', Ostap 'главный концессионер' / 'технический директор' and Vorobyaninov 'директор-учредитель концессии', alternating with the plainer 'компаньоны'. A концессия in 1920s usage was the NEP-specific licence under which a foreign firm (Lena Goldfields, Harriman's manganese, Hammer's Alapayevsk asbestos, Krupp's Manych farm) was allowed to run a state-owned enterprise for profit, per the Sovnarkom decree of 23 Nov 1920; they were headline news and a byword for capitalist money-making in Soviet Russia until the Main Concessions Committee was wound up around 1930. So the joke is that two private jewel-hunters style themselves a quasi-official foreign-capital enterprise, complete with percentages and 'соцстрах'. Both published English versions keep it: John Richardson (1971, lib.ru) uses 'concessionaires' ~65 times and 'partners' for компаньоны, and Anne O. Fisher (Northwestern UP, 2011) also writes 'the concessionaires'. For Chinese, the established historiographic term for NEP concessions is 租让制/租让企业 (Lenin's 1921 租让 principles), not 特许经营 (which now reads as franchising); for Japanese, Soviet-era concessions are conventionally 利権 (e.g. 北樺太石油利権) or コンセッション. I could not retrieve the actual in-text renderings of the Chinese (徐昌翰 1985, 张佩文 2004, 白桦熊 2022) or Japanese (江川卓 1969) translations; those are inferred from the historical terminology, not verified. The prompt's reference to 'Durov and VKontakte' and 'a Russian reader around 2013' does not match this 1928 novel and was ignored.

rendering.ja: 利権者たち / 共同経営者たち

value.note_for_reader: A 'concession' (концессия) was the NEP-era licence letting a foreign firm run a Soviet state enterprise for profit; Ostap grandly styles the two-man jewel hunt as one, so the narrator calls the pair 'concessionaires'.
value.rationale: Keeps the denotation (a NEP concession, via the period term in each language: concession / 租让 / 利権) and the mock-official register, with a plain business word for компаньоны so the two names stay distinct; gives up the automatic 1928 recognition that the joke was topical, which the one-line note supplies. 特许经营者 and 利権屋 were rejected: the first shifts to modern franchising, the second adds a slangy 'profiteer' sneer the deadpan narrator does not have.

value.finding: In the novel (ch. XXI 'Экзекуция', auction scene) the word is a garment: the auctioneer's beard falls onto 'толстовку русского коверкота'. A толстовка of the 1910s–20s is a long, loose men's blouse worn outside the trousers, usually belted, with dense gathers or pleats, a standing collar, buttoned front and chest pockets — a cross between a soldier's гимнастёрка and a peasant shirt, named after the loose shirt in which the aged Tolstoy was endlessly photographed; the word itself entered Russian only in the late 1910s and Tolstoy never used it. In the early Soviet years it was popular for its 'democratic', anti-bourgeois look (as opposed to a suit) among office workers, intellectuals, writers and artists, and by 1930 it had gone out of fashion except among artists; in 1928 it read as the standard, slightly earnest uniform of a Soviet служащий, so a bearded auctioneer in loud checked trousers plus a covert-cloth толстовка is a mildly absurd mix. The modern sense 'sweatshirt/hoodie' dates only from the 1980s–90s and must not leak in. Existing English coverage (Wikipedia, the Master and Margarita annotations, the standard shop name) uses 'Tolstoy blouse' / 'Tolstoy shirt'; Japanese sources either transliterate トルストフカ or explain it via ルバシカ and give no fixed descriptive term; Chinese sources use 托尔斯泰衬衫 for the Tolstoy-style shirt. I could not retrieve the exact sentence in the Richardson or Fisher English translations, so their choice is unverified. (The brief's mention of Durov/VKontakte and 2013 does not apply to this 1928 term.)
value.note_for_reader: Tolstovka: the loose, belted, pleated over-shirt Tolstoy wore; in the 1920s the plain 'democratic' dress of Soviet clerks and intellectuals — not today's sweatshirt.
value.rationale: All three keep the denotation (a period garment named for Tolstoy) and the neutral register, and a reader who knows Tolstoy's portraits gets the image; what is given up is the 1928 connotation of a bland Soviet-office uniform, which the one-line note restores. 'Blouse' rather than 'shirt' in English signals the loose belted cut; zh and ja follow the only existing usages found and stay transparent for the target reader.

value.finding: ЗАГС is the acronym of 'запись актов гражданского состояния' (registration of acts of civil status): the local Soviet office that registers births, marriages, divorces and deaths. It was created by the Sovnarkom decree of 18 December 1917 on civil marriage and the 1918 code, which took these functions away from the church's parish 'metric books' and made only state registration legally valid, so by 1928 the word was everyday, lower-case Russian (ru.wikipedia writes 'загс' as a common noun; 'пойти в загс' still means 'to get married'). In chapter 1 the original reads 'служил в загсе, где ведал столом регистрации смертей и браков' and the joke turns on the 'толстые книги' in which everything born or married that day is written down: the ex-marshal of the nobility now keeps the secular successor of the parish register in a provincial town. Richardson's 1961 English translation renders it simply 'registry office' (no acronym); Fisher's 2011 version could not be checked online. Japanese dictionaries give the standard gloss 戸籍登録課, reading ザークス (kotobank Russian-Japanese dictionary), and ja.wikipedia lists ЗАГС as 戸籍登録機関; a Chinese ebook translation found online domesticates it as 民政局 (a PRC civil-affairs bureau), which is anachronistic. The prompt's mention of 'Durov and VKontakte around 2013' does not apply to this term and was ignored.
value.note_for_reader: ZAGS: Soviet acronym for the office of 'civil-status acts', which in 1917–18 replaced church parish registers as the only legal record of births, marriages and deaths.
value.rationale: All three keep the denotation (a state office for births, marriages, deaths) and carry the acronym once so later bare 'ZAGS'/'ザークス' and the thick-ledger joke land; the Japanese uses the dictionary-standard 戸籍登録 and reading ザークス rather than 登記/ザーグス, and the Chinese uses 民事登记 instead of 户籍登记 because 户籍 would make a PRC reader think of hukou residence registration. Given up: the flat bureaucratic sound of a Soviet acronym as an ordinary word, which no target language reproduces without a gloss.

value.finding: Предводитель дворянства was the elected head of the nobility of a district (уезд) or province (губерния), instituted by Catherine II's 1785 Charter to the Nobility and abolished in 1917: chosen by the noble assembly for a three-year term, unpaid, confirmed by the governor (district) or the emperor (province), chairing the zemstvo assembly, school and conscription boards, so that the district marshal was the de facto head of his district. To a 1928 or 2013 Russian reader it is the quintessential 'former person' title: a gentry grandee of the old regime, now an ex-. In the novel Ostap's habitual vocative is the bare 'предводитель' ('Вам, предводитель, пора уже лечиться электричеством'; 'а вы, предводитель, не жмите девочку'), he mocks 'для предводителя дворянства у вас слишком мелкие масштабы', and at the auction escalates to 'Не бойтесь, гофмаршал!'; I could not find the exact wording 'Молитесь, предводитель' on Wikisource, where the auction line reads 'Молитесь на меня, молитесь!'. English coverage (Richardson 1961, Wikipedia) uniformly uses 'marshal of the nobility'; Japanese uses 貴族団長 (ja.wikipedia article; Anna Karenina character lists give 県貴族団長; Japanese summaries of the novel call Vorobyaninov 元貴族団長); Chinese editions of the novel (徐昌翰, 后浪 2022 description) and the People's Literature Anna Karenina use 首席贵族 / 省首席贵族, as does Chinese historiography (张宗华), while 贵族长 is rarer. I could not verify how Richardson or Fisher render the bare vocative.

rendering.en: marshal of the nobility (full title); bare vocative: Marshal
rendering.zh: 首席贵族（全称）；奥斯塔普单独呼唤时：首席
rendering.ja: 貴族団長（正式名）；オスタップの呼びかけ：団長

value.note_for_reader: Marshal of the nobility (предводитель дворянства): the elected head of a district's gentry under the tsars, an unpaid but powerful local dignitary; abolished in 1917. Ostap's 'Marshal' is a jeer at Vorobyaninov's lost rank.
value.rationale: Kept the established denotation in all three languages (marshal of the nobility / 首席贵族 / 貴族団長) and a one-word vocative in each (Marshal / 首席 / 団長) whose slightly wrong secondary sense (military marshal, CEO-style 'chief', troupe leader) reproduces Ostap's mock-solemn deflation; gave up the transparency of 'leader of the nobility' and, in Chinese, the shorter but less attested 贵族长.

value.finding: A милиционер is a rank-and-file member of the милиция, the ordinary uniformed police of Soviet Russia. The name comes from a Provisional Government decree of 17 April 1917 and was reaffirmed by the Bolsheviks on 10 November 1917 as the 'Workers' and Peasants' Militia', deliberately avoiding the tsarist word полиция, which connoted autocratic repression; the intended association was with popular self-organisation rather than a professional state force. By 1928 the word was fully lexicalised and neutral: in the novel a милиционер is simply the man at the crossroads with a traffic baton, a cop to be edged past by an ice-cream seller or a con man, with no overtone of armed irregulars. Russia only renamed the force полиция on 1 March 2011, so for every Russian reader before then милиционер was the plain everyday word for policeman. In English, the 1961 Richardson translation uses 'militiaman' throughout (e.g. the ice-cream seller who 'squinted timorously at the militiaman ... regulating the traffic'); English Wikipedia notes the institution is usually left as 'militsiya' or glossed 'police'. Japanese coverage renders the institution ミリツィヤ（民警） and Chinese coverage 苏联民警 (alongside 苏联民兵), so 民警 is the established rendering in both. I could not verify Anne Fisher's (2011) choice directly.
value.note_for_reader: Soviet police were called the 'militia' (милиция) from 1917 to 2011 to mark a break with the tsarist 'police'; a милиционер is an ordinary uniformed policeman, not an irregular.
value.rationale: For English I keep denotation and the neutral everyday register at the cost of the Soviet-specific connotation, since 'militiaman' (Richardson's choice) suggests armed irregulars to a non-specialist; one note at first occurrence carries the lost nuance. For Chinese and Japanese 民警 keeps all three: it is the established term for the Soviet militsiya in both languages and reads as an ordinary neighbourhood policeman (the PRC's own 人民警察 are also called 民警), so no note is needed there.

value.finding: Ostap Bender's recurring catchphrase (first in ch. 6, then chs. 12, 21, 30, 40 etc.), always in the same courtroom-chairman idiom as his 'Лёд тронулся, господа присяжные заседатели!': Ostap casts himself as presiding judge and Vorobyaninov as the jury, so in ch. 21 'Заседание продолжается! Слышите? Вы! Присяжный заседатель!' turns 'juryman' into a jeer at his useless partner. Dushenko's Большой словарь цитат and dslov.ru trace the formula to Charles Dupuy, president of the French Chamber of Deputies, who after Vaillant's bomb on 9 Dec 1893 said 'Messieurs, la séance continue!'; by 1928 it was a stock phrase of unflappable officialdom that Ilf and Petrov hand to a con man. In Russian it became a proverb meaning 'the business goes on, nothing has stopped us' and is listed in every dictionary of крылатые слова. Established renderings: John Richardson's English (lib.ru, cited by Wikipedia) uses 'The hearing is continued' throughout and 'Hey you, member of the jury?' for the ch. 21 insult; the 2022 Shanghai Translation edition (tr. 白桦熊) is marketed with the catchphrase as '庭审继续进行！' alongside '陪审员先生们'; no Japanese wording from Egawa Taku's 1966/1969 translation could be verified online.
value.note_for_reader: Ostap's catchphrase apes a presiding judge or chairman (famously Charles Dupuy's 'Messieurs, la séance continue!' after the 1893 bomb in the French Chamber); he addresses his partner as the jury, so 'juryman' here is a taunt.
value.rationale: All three keep the courtroom frame so the phrase can sit beside 'gentlemen of the jury / 陪审员先生们 / 陪審員諸君' and the 'juryman' insult; en and zh bind the published renderings (Richardson; Shanghai Translation 2022) rather than the flatter 'session/meeting continues', which loses the jury pairing. The Dupuy allusion and the proverb status are given up (a one-line note carries them); ja is a defensible novel wording since Egawa's text could not be checked.

value.term: «Большевики пишут письмо Чемберлену» (по Репину: «Запорожцы пишут письмо султану»)
value.finding: In the Stargorod chapters Bender considers offering the local children's commission an 'as yet unpainted but brilliantly conceived' picture, hoping for some 400 rubles, and worries only that it would be technically hard to show Kalinin in a papakha and white burka and Chicherin bare to the waist. The model is Repin's 'Запорожцы' (1880–91, Russian Museum), popularly called 'Запорожцы пишут письмо турецкому султану'; the standard English title is 'Reply of the Zaporozhian Cossacks', with 'Cossacks Writing a Letter to the Turkish Sultan' as an accepted alternate; ja: 『トルコのスルタンへ手紙を書くザポロージャ・コサック』; zh: 《扎波罗热哥萨克致土耳其苏丹的回信》 / 《扎波罗热人写信给土耳其苏丹》 (older art books: 《查波罗什人写信给苏丹王》). Chamberlain is Sir Austen Chamberlain, British Foreign Secretary, whose note of 23 Feb 1927 demanded the USSR stop anti-British propaganda and aid to the Chinese revolution; Pravda's 'Our reply to Chamberlain!' became the slogan of the year, even naming an Osoaviakhim air-fleet fund. The joke is doubly topical: a 1923 'Krasny Perets' cartoon had already posed Bolshevik leaders (including Kalinin and Chicherin) as Repin's Cossacks writing to Lord Curzon, and 'Krokodil' ran 'Workers Write a Reply to Chamberlain' in 1927, so a 1928 reader saw Bender plagiarising a well-worn agitprop cliché to milk a state committee. The English, Chinese and Japanese translations of the novel do not appear to have a canonical rendering online; the Repin title in each language is the fixed point.

https://zh.wikipedia.org/zh-hans/扎波罗热哥萨克致土耳其苏丹的回信

rendering.zh: 《布尔什维克给张伯伦写信》，仿列宾名画《扎波罗热人给土耳其苏丹写信》

value.note_for_reader: Austen Chamberlain, British Foreign Secretary, sent Moscow an ultimatum-like note in Feb 1927; 'Our reply to Chamberlain!' was the Soviet slogan of the year, and cartoons had already recast Repin's laughing Cossacks as Bolshevik leaders (Kalinin, the head of state; Chicherin, the foreign commissar).
value.rationale: Denotation and the mock-solemn register are kept by mirroring the novel's own descriptive title of the Repin picture in each language's established form; the connotation that Bender is recycling a stale agitprop cliché of 1927 cannot survive without the note, which carries it.

value.finding: Ilf and Petrov's fixed narratorial epithet for Ostap Bender in Двенадцать стульев (1928; it titles chapter 5) and Золотой телёнок (1931; it titles chapter 1). 'Комбинатор' in 1920s usage meant a man of 'комбинации' — clever, not-quite-honest deals — and 'великий' gives it mock-epic solemnity; Russian dictionaries define the phrase as 'ловкий пройдоха, добивающийся успеха путём сложных операций, уловок, мошенничества' and note it became a proverbial catchphrase, ironic or disapproving, for any slick schemer. English translators split: Richardson (1961, the standard edition) uses 'the smooth operator' (chapter 5 title), Malamuth's Golden Calf 'the great schemer', Fisher (2009/2011) 'the grand strategist', while Wikipedia glosses it 'The Great Combinator / The Great Schemer'. Chinese editions likewise vary: 张佩文 (人民文学 2004) 伟大谋士, 白桦熊 (上海译文 2022) 了不起的幕僚, with 伟大的谋略家 common in Chinese commentary. No fixed Japanese epithet was found in coverage of the 江川卓 (1966/1969) or 上田進 (1957) translations; reviews describe Bender as 大詐欺師 or 策士. The prompt's mention of Durov/VKontakte and 2013 does not apply to this term; the 1928 novel context was used.
value.note_for_reader: Великий комбинатор, 'the Grand Schemer': the narrator's mock-heroic title for Bender, now a Russian byword for a charming con man.
value.rationale: All three keep the mock-solemn 'great/grand + agent noun' shape so the epithet is recognisable across the parallel columns and stays fixed; 'Grand Schemer' is a near-variant of the established Malamuth/Wikipedia 'great schemer' with Fisher's 'grand', and 谋略家/策士 both carry 'strategist' with a shady undertone. Given up: Richardson's idiomatic but un-grand 'smooth operator', the 1920s flavour of 'комбинация', and the phrase's proverbial afterlife, which no target reader can feel without the note.

value.finding: Финагент is the Soviet-era clipped compound 'финансовый агент' (Ushakov marks it 'нов.'), the lowest rung of the Narkomfin district tax staff: the 1925 Regulation on external tax supervision set out фининспектор, their assistants, and финагенты, and assigned the actual collection of payments (взимание платежей) to the agents, while inspectors assessed income. So a финагент is the man who physically calls on shopkeepers and mattress-owners to take the money, not an auditor or a broker. In chapter XVII ('Уважайте матрацы, граждане!') Ilf and Petrov use him as a stock figure of NEP everyday life who arrives 'в целях фискальных' and, having gathered the tax like a bee gathering the spring nectar-flow, 'с радостным гулом улетает в свой участковый улей'. For a 1928 reader the word carried mild dread and ridicule (cf. Mayakovsky's fininspektor): the petty state functionary who materialises as soon as you own anything. Richardson's 1961 English (the only full text online) renders the same passage 'Having collected his tax like a bumblebee gathering spring honey, the tax collector flies away with a joyful hum to his district hive', and 'income-tax collector' in the preceding sentence and in chapter III. I could not locate the Chinese (张佩文 / 白桦熊) or Japanese (江川卓, 1969) wording of this sentence online; the zh/ja choices below are therefore mine.
value.rationale: All three keep the denotation (a low-level official who comes to collect, which is what the bee-and-hive image needs) and the established English precedent; 'tax collector' / 收税员 / 徴税吏 deliberately rank him below the proposed 'inspector' / 稽查员 / 官, which is closer to fact. What is given up is the Soviet acronym flavour of фин-, which no target language can carry without a note, and which the mock-solemn sentence supplies anyway.

value.finding: Not a song title in itself but a line from the refrain of the 1915 drawing-room romance «Молчи, грусть, молчи» (words Anatoly D'Aktil/Frenkel, music Grigory Berezovsky; the commentary in the Odessky–Feldman-annotated text credits B. Grodzky): «Молчи, грусть, молчи, / Не тронь старых ран, / Сказки любви дорогой / Не вернуть никогда, никогда». «дорогой» is 'dear, precious', not 'expensive'. The same two lines became the titles of Pyotr Chardynin's 1918 two-part melodrama starring Vera Kholodnaya, whose part two was released as «Сказка любви дорогой»; the annotators say the novel may allude to either the romance or the film. In the chapter at the Furniture Museum, Ippolit Matveevich, aged 52, exchanges names with Liza Kalachova and the line pops into his head as he peers at her «простенькое лицо» — for a 1928 reader it was instantly recognisable pre-war salon kitsch, the mental soundtrack of a fossil, and the deadpan narration undercuts it at once with his grabbing her hand. Richardson's English (1961) renders it 'A tale of true love'; Fisher's 2011 rendering could not be checked online. The film is 'Be Silent, My Sorrow, Be Silent' in English Wikipedia and 「黙れ、わが悲しみ、黙れ」 in Japanese Wikipedia; no Chinese or Japanese rendering of the second-part title or of the refrain line was found.
sources: https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/ヴェーラ・ホロドナヤ
value.note_for_reader: A line from the refrain of the 1915 salon romance 'Hush, my sorrow, hush' (Молчи, грусть, молчи), also the title of a 1918 Vera Kholodnaya melodrama — pre-revolutionary sentimental kitsch surfacing in Vorobyaninov's head.
value.rationale: All three keep the denotation (a tale of dear/precious love) and the kitsch register of a sentimental song title in quotation marks: the inverted 'Love So Dear', the Chinese 爱情童话 cliché, and the archaic Japanese いとしき all signal old-fashioned sentimentality; what is given up is the recognition effect — the target reader cannot hear the melody or the Kholodnaya film — which the one-line note supplies.
